Arbitrarily

/ar-bih-TRAIR-uh-lee/ · adverb

Hear It

What It Means

Arbitrarily means in a way based on random choice or personal whim rather than any reason, rule, or system.

The substitute teacher assigned seats arbitrarily, pulling names from a coffee mug without a glance at the seating chart.

Worked Example

A new manager at a shipping warehouse decided which employees got weekend shifts by dealing out playing cards: red card, you worked; black card, you stayed home. Seniority, family obligations, and even who had volunteered made no difference at all. Workers did not object to weekend shifts themselves, but they resented that the schedule was set arbitrarily, with no reason or rule anyone could point to. A rotation list posted the next month fixed the problem overnight.

The shifts were assigned by random card colors rather than by any rule or reason, which is exactly what it means to decide something arbitrarily.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

randomly: in a way determined by chance rather than plan

whimsically: on a playful, fanciful impulse; arbitrarily is the harsher word, criticizing a choice made with no reason or rule behind it

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

systematically: according to a fixed plan or method

methodically: in a careful, orderly, step-by-step way

Where it sits · how little reason or rule governs it — casually → arbitrarily → lawlessly

casually vs. arbitrarily: Doing something casually just means doing it in a relaxed, informal way, while doing it arbitrarily means there is no reason or rule behind the choice at all.

lawlessly vs. arbitrarily: A rule applied arbitrarily follows whim instead of reason, but a rule applied lawlessly ignores even the authority of law itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — arbitr

Root — arbitr: from Latin arbiter, a judge or umpire who decided disputes by personal judgment

Suffix — -ary

Suffix — -ary: relating to, of the nature of

Suffix — -ly

Suffix — -ly: in the manner of; forms adverbs

Put it together

Put it together: Arbitrarily is built on Latin arbiter, the judge or umpire who settled Roman disputes by his own personal judgment. Add the suffixes -ary and -ly, and the word describes acting the way such a judge might at his most unchecked: by one's own whim, answering to no rule.

Use the root in a new word: arbitration

Use the root in a new word: arbitration: The two firms settled their contract fight through arbitration, handing the decision to a private judge, the very arbiter named by the Latin root.

Word Choice

neutral, academic and everyday register

Arbitrarily is an adverb, so it describes how an action is done: rules enforced arbitrarily, numbers chosen arbitrarily, prices set arbitrarily. It usually carries a critical edge, hinting that a decision deserved a reason and got none.
